VBO:0200833.summary: Affectionate and sociable, the Long-Haired Whippet combines the intensity of a sighthound with an unusually responsive approach to working with people. Coursing, agility and scentwork are among its modern activities. Developed in the United States from the 1960s, this distinct coated breed adopted the name Windsprite in 2017.
VBO:0200833.shortDescription: A sociable, responsive coated sighthound, the Windsprite brings athletic intensity to coursing and agility.

sources.title: International Windsprite Club — About the breed
sources.evidence: The IWC identifies an independent mid-sized coated sighthound founded in the United States from the 1960s, closely related to but distinct from Whippets. It explicitly describes sociability, affection and added biddability, and lists members’ coursing, agility, scentwork, running and hiking activities. These support the character opening, modern activities and US development date; promotional suitability promises are excluded.

sources.title: International Windsprite Club — Breed standard
sources.evidence: The IWC temperament clause describes an easygoing, calm, dignified and gentle dog that is intense in the field. Its conformation clauses document rose ears preferred, lean sighthound proportions, a soft straight/slightly wavy coat with chest/leg/tail feathering, and a long tapered tail reaching at least the hocks, sweeping gently upward at the tip and not carried high above the back. These support the sourced morphology and new pose; the original’s handler and show setting will not be reproduced.

sources.title: International Windsprite Club — Breed name change: Windsprite
sources.evidence: The club’s passed membership motion explicitly changes the name from Longhaired Whippet to Windsprite as of January 1, 2017; this supports the catalog-to-modern-name identity and final history sentence. It does not identify Silken Windhound as the same breed.

VBO:0200884.summary: Sociable and often eager for company, Cockapoos can enjoy learning, games and close involvement with their people; some become unsettled when left alone. The miniature version traces its size to Miniature Poodle ancestry, paired originally with a Cocker Spaniel. Working or show Cocker ancestry and later generations bring variation in energy, temperament and coat, even within a litter.
VBO:0200884.shortDescription: A company-loving Cocker–Miniature Poodle cross whose energy, coat and temperament vary with its ancestry.

sources.title: Cockapoo Club of Great Britain — What is a Cockapoo?
sources.evidence: CCGB explicitly defines a Miniature Cockapoo by a Miniature Poodle parent and describes F1, F2 and backcross generations, differences among American/English show and English working Cocker ancestry, and variation in size, coat and temperament. These support the cross definition and generational variation. Parent-specific skills, intelligence, hybrid-vigour and allergy claims are not transferred to the cross or individual.

sources.title: British Cockapoo Society — Thinking of getting a Cockapoo
sources.evidence: BCS describes Cockapoos as generally friendly and company-loving, often enjoying time with a preferred person, learning/training and games; it notes that some become upset on separation and exceptions exist. It gives miniature adults an average 11–14 inch range. These support qualified social/learning/separation wording; they do not guarantee an individual’s temperament or the pictured dog’s precise measured height.

VBO:0200892.summary: In one UK owner survey, Labradoodles were more excitable than Labradors but had fewer separation-related problems than Poodles. The miniature version draws its size from Miniature Poodle ancestry within the original Labrador–Poodle cross. It is distinct from the separately developed Australian Labradoodle, whose ancestry includes several additional breeds.
VBO:0200892.shortDescription: A Labrador–Miniature Poodle cross with variable temperament, distinct from the developed Australian Labradoodle.

sources.title: Poodle-cross behaviour: UK owner survey (PLOS One, 2026)
sources.evidence: The 2026 UK study collected owner C-BARQ responses in March2023, including583 Labradoodles and251 reported Miniature Poodle progenitors. Adjusted Labradoodle comparisons showed more excitability than Labrador Retrievers (p<.001) and fewer separation-related problems than pooled Poodles (p=.008). The study defines Labradoodles as Labrador Retriever×Poodle, records Miniature Poodle ancestry and pools Poodle sizes. The summary explicitly reports one owner survey; it does not infer an individual’s temperament, health or intelligence. Size groups and miniature-cross behaviour were not analyzed as separate results; this limitation belongs here and in source notes.

sources.title: Australian Labradoodle Association — Parent breeds
sources.evidence: The Australian Labradoodle Association describes six breeds in Australian Labradoodle development. This is used only to distinguish the developed Australian type from the ordinary two-parent Labrador–Poodle cross named by the study and owner caption; it supplies no conformation or behavioural claim for this ordinary Miniature Labradoodle.

VBO:0008005.summary: Lively and strongly drawn to scent, the Bulgarian Barak follows fresh trails with stamina and a deep, carrying voice. It tends to bond closely with its owner while remaining wary of unfamiliar people. Bulgaria’s rough-coated hunting population developed into this named breed through local selection; its modern club adopted a standard in 2004.
VBO:0008005.shortDescription: A lively Bulgarian scent hound with a deep voice, close attachment to its owner and a persistent hunting drive.

sources.title: National Bulgarian Barak Club — Breed standard
sources.evidence: Actual national Barak club standard Use and Behaviour specifies fresh-trail scent work, endurance across climate/terrain, lively hunting drive, attachment to owner, distrust of unfamiliar people and a deep clear far-carrying voice. The history supports local selection without adopting ancient migration narratives; morphology documents elongated dry sturdy frame, drop ears, harsh slightly wavy yellow/red hair with grey/black saddle, beard/brows and low-set tapering hock-length natural tail carried as a sabre when excited. Blank FCI number does not support FCI recognition.

sources.title: National Bulgarian Barak Club — Club history and events
sources.evidence: Actual club events/history body states the breed standard was adopted at its general assembly on27March2004. February2004 Bulgarian federation membership is a separate club event, not international FCI recognition. Supports the modern standard date only.

VBO:0008006.summary: Persistent and energetic on a trail, the Bulgarian Ludogorian Hound combines strong scenting ability with a clear baritone voice and a close bond to its owner. Its passion for game can make it hard to interrupt during a hunt. Long associated with Bulgaria’s Ludogorie region, this smooth-coated hound was shaped by selection for tracking wild boar through rough, densely wooded terrain.
VBO:0008006.shortDescription: An energetic boar hound from Bulgaria, with a persistent hunting drive, clear baritone voice and close owner bond.

sources.title: National Bulgarian Hound Club — Characteristics and modern development
sources.evidence: Actual national Bulgarian Hound Club body states specialized boar hunting, strong smell/orientation/energy/endurance across terrain/climate, passion for game that sometimes makes behaviour difficult to control, prolonged pursuit and a clear velvety baritone voice; work in rough mountain terrain with dense forest. This supports persistence and difficulty interrupting during hunting without asserting aggression or suitability. Ancient Celtic/Asian ancestry and claimed international recognition are excluded.

sources.title: Bulgarian Republican Cynology Union — Ludogorian Hound standard
sources.evidence: Actual BRKS history/standard locates largest population in northeastern Ludogorie, describes prolonged persistent pursuit, scenting ability, lively temperament and attachment to owner. Use specializes boar hunting and densely wooded rough terrain. Exact morphology is medium elongated lean strong black/tan smooth coat, dark eyes/drop rounded ears, thick-based tapering hock-length natural tail relaxed down or at/slightly above topline in action; no full wheel curl or white tip. No ancient ancestry or verified FCI recognition is adopted.

VBO:0008064.summary: Gentle in disposition yet agile in action, the Jeju native dog is known for hunting ability that draws on keen hearing, scent and vision. It comes from a conserved Jeju Island population whose local bloodlines are the focus of preservation work, with genetic diversity a particular concern.
VBO:0008064.shortDescription: A gentle but agile Jeju Island hunting dog, with keen senses and a distinct population maintained through conservation.

sources.title: National Institute of Animal Science — Jeju native dog, 2019
sources.evidence: Actual NIAS25July2019 primary body explicitly says gentle disposition, agile action and developed hearing/smell/vision with hunting ability. It describes Jeju Province preservation and genetic analysis of20 conserved dogs, comparison with native populations, distinct bloodlines and need to secure diversity. Managed49 is a2019 count, not current; no NationalMonument or universal Korean-village identity claim. NIAS Type2NC source photo is excluded from all morphology/image inputs; textual evidence only.

sources.title: Rural Development Administration — Companion dogs, 2011
sources.evidence: Actual RDA Interrobang43,23November2011, printedp5/PDFp9 describes agile Jeju hunting dog with broad forehead, foxlike muzzle, coarse hair and erect ears. Used for exact nonvisual hunting context and morphology confirmation only; no RDA/NIAS image used as generation input.

VBO:0200044.summary: Cautious and often shy with unfamiliar people, the American Dingo or Carolina Dog need not seek close contact with strangers. Its breed history grew from free-ranging dogs that I. Lehr Brisbin studied in the southeastern United States in the 1970s.
VBO:0200044.shortDescription: A cautious, often shy dog from southeastern US free-ranging populations, studied and named in the 1970s.

sources.title: United Kennel Club — Carolina Dog standard
sources.evidence: UKC’s Characteristics describes a generally shy/suspicious nature and says a Carolina Dog need not be outgoing or enjoy physical contact with strangers. History specifically describes Brisbin’s 1970s observations/trapping of southeastern US free-ranging dogs and their naming as Carolina Dogs; earlier North American ancestry is a hypothesis requiring further genetic study. This supports the qualified character/history prose without promising eventual sociability or asserting settled ancient descent. The standard documents a lean rectangular adult frame, upright mobile ears, ginger/cream colouring and a long tail with an ideal open fishhook near the endpoint, never a complete curl touching the back. These support new standing morphology; the exact prone source’s feet are not claimed to be standing.

VBO:0200291.summary: Carea Leonés dogs are attentive, quick to learn and strongly focused on their handlers while working livestock. They developed around León’s sheep flocks, guiding animals through cultivated ground and fallow fields. Their energetic, balanced movement lets them change pace and direction readily, with the trotting endurance of a dog built for long working days.
VBO:0200291.shortDescription: Attentive Leonese sheepdogs, quick to learn and responsive to their handlers through long days of flock work.

sources.title: RSCE — Perro Leonés de Pastor / Carea Leonés
sources.evidence: Exact synonym crosswalk CareaLeonés to nationallyrecognized PerroLeonésdePastor. Behavioursection: attention/learning, strong herding disposition, lasting working engagement and handlerfocus. HistoryNorthernSpain/Leóncropland-fallowsheep management. Morphology49–50cmmale47–48female±1,size17–21kgmale15–19female,body1:1.13–1.14,foldedears,mediumcoat,complete tailrestbelowhock; no primaryreference override.

VBO:0200449.summary: Dogue Brasileiro dogs are active, attentive and observant, often showing a serious manner with strangers and a gentler expression with their own people. Developed in Brazil by Pedro Pessoa Ribeiro Dantas for guard work, the breed standard values discipline and balance. For a championship title, dogs must pass an assessment of courage and control.
VBO:0200449.shortDescription: Active, observant Brazilian guard dogs whose standard emphasizes discipline, balanced character and controlled courage.

sources.title: CBKC — Dogue Brasileiro standard
sources.evidence: P2 exact guardfunction and developer named; P3 activeattentiveobservant,seriouswithstrangersgentleowner, balanceddiscipline andno gratuitousaggression ideal. P6championship characterappreciation requires courage/control; no individualdanger-free guarantee. P4natural semidrop ears, P5intacttail permitted longer than dockedoption. No inventedcreationyear or parentalcharacterblend. Actualp5CAUDA: thick, medium insertion, above back during movement with very slightly concave posture; docking optional at approximately1.2headlength, intact tail approximately1.8headlength. Actualp4 natural ears semi-fallen frontolaterally. Source visibly docked tail is documented separately; new intact tail morphology derives from permitted intact standard, not source tail appearance.

VBO:0200473.summary: East-European Shepherd Dogs are attentive, self-confident and active workers, with a balanced manner and a readiness to learn. Their development in Russia focused on service dogs able to work across sharply different climates. A central military and sporting-dog school was established in 1924, and the first East-European Shepherd standard followed in 1955.
VBO:0200473.shortDescription: Attentive, confident service shepherds, selected for endurance, adaptability and a ready response to training.

sources.title: Russian Kynological Federation — East-European Shepherd standard
sources.evidence: Exactdistinct Russianuniversalservicebreed. Behaviour balanced,active,selfconfident,attentive,easilytrained. Historicalselection for varied climates/working ability; militarysportdogschool established1924, servicepopulationincludespure/mixedlocalstocks, not merely parentbreed enlarged. No individual protection/suitability promise. Actual RKF full historical body states the Central experimental military/sporting dog school established1924 and first East-European Shepherd standard15September1955. Dates describe service-breeding institutions/standard, not a modern individual pedigree or unbroken ancient lineage.

sources.title: CBKC — East-European Shepherd standard
sources.evidence: Current2026 official Portuguese standard corroborates identity, balancedactiveconfidentattentiveeasytraining character andutilityguardcompanion work. Source fromactualCBKCbreedindex data-file link, not guessedPDF. Retain currentversion independent of RKF2014valid/2020approval dates.

VBO:0201020.summary: Sweet, affectionate and playful with familiar people, the Argentine Pila can remain distrustful of strangers. It tends to learn household routines readily and moves with notable agility, including strong jumping ability. Modern preservation in Salta led to a national association standard in 2007, distinguishing this local hairless population from the other American hairless breeds.
VBO:0201020.shortDescription: An affectionate, playful Argentine companion, agile on its feet and inclined to be distrustful of unfamiliar people.

sources.title: Asociación Canina Argentina — Perro Pila standard, updated March 2024
sources.evidence: ACA’s Generalidades describes the Argentine Pila as sweet, affectionate and playful with familiar household members, distrustful of strangers, and readily learning household rules. Movimiento specifically documents exceptional agility for jumping. The page dates ACA standard approval to October 2007 and credits Salta pioneers, Mónica Cassels’s preservation work and Coronel Moldes events; its introduction states an aim to distinguish the local Pila from other American hairless breeds. These statements support the summary and short description. ACA is distinct from Argentina’s FCA and the FCI; no FCA/FCI recognition is claimed. Speculative common ancestry and Dobermann/Poodle ancestry, allergy, health and universal child/animal safety statements on the page are excluded.
